title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment
tagline: The Jung-typology career assessment as the self-knowledge layer beneath every career decision: what the instrument measures, what it doesn't, and how to turn a type into a working plan.

domains.name: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment
domains.summary: The Jung-typology assessment as a self-knowledge instrument: what it measures, what it doesn't, and how to convert a type into career fit and a development plan — independent study, no affiliation with any assessment provider.

scenarios.title: The hiring-screen misuse
scenarios.situation: A hiring manager asks candidates to take the Jung typology test and rejects everyone who doesn't test as ENTJ — 'we only hire commanders.' You know the instrument: 72 forced-choice questions sorting preferences across four dichotomies (Extraversion/Introversion, Sensing/Intuition, Thinking/Feeling, Judging/Perceiving) into 16 types.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with using the assessment this way?
choices: The instrument measures preferences — how people prefer to take in information and make decisions — not ability, competence, or job performance; using it as a hiring filter is both a misuse of what it measures and unfair to candidates whose strengths lie outside one type.
Nothing is wrong; ENTJs are objectively the best leaders so the filter is efficient.
The only problem is the 72-question length; a shorter test would make the filter fine.
The problem is that candidates can lie; with a lie-detector version the filter would work.
scenarios.why: Preference is not performance: an INTJ and an ESFP can both be excellent engineers, and the test says nothing about skill, experience, or motivation. The instrument's own design purpose is self-knowledge for development and career reflection — converting it into a hiring gate confuses 'how someone prefers to work' with 'whether they can do the work,' and it screens out strong candidates for no valid reason.
scenarios.hint: Does the test measure what you CAN do, or what you PREFER?

scenarios.title: Reading your own result
scenarios.situation: Your assessment result reads: INTJ — Introverted (38%), Intuitive (3%), Thinking (6%), Judging (38%). The write-up calls INTJs 'systems builders' who prize competence and independence. You're excited, but two of the four preferences are marginal — nearly 50/50.
scenarios.prompt: How should you interpret the marginal preferences?
choices: Treat the percentages as preference clarity, not as grades: a 3% Intuition preference means characteristics of both INTJ and ISTJ may apply to you — work with the whole profile including the near-ties, not just the four-letter label.
Ignore the percentages; the four letters are definitive and the numbers are decoration.
Retake the test until all four preferences are strong, then trust the result.
The marginal scores mean the test failed and the result should be discarded.
scenarios.why: The percentage is the strength of the preference signal on that sitting: 38% is moderate clarity, 3% is essentially no preference. Near-tie dimensions mean you genuinely draw on both sides — planning with the ISTJ description alongside the INTJ one gives a truer picture than the label alone. The working-styles view uses the full profile; the four letters are just shorthand.
scenarios.hint: If Intuition is 3%, which other type's description is worth reading too?

scenarios.title: Type to role-family mapping
scenarios.situation: A career counselor maps your ISTJ result — Introverted, Sensing, Thinking, Judging — to role families. The write-up describes ISTJs as thorough, dependable, practical, and organized, thriving on clear processes and schedules. You're choosing between two offers: site-reliability operations with strict runbooks, and developer-evangelist doing conference talks and demos.
scenarios.prompt: Which fit does the type suggest, and with what caveat?
choices: The ISTJ working style aligns with the SRE operations role — structured processes, reliability, checklists, deep focus — while the evangelist role leans on extraverted, spontaneous strengths; the caveat is that type suggests energy fit and working style, not capability — you could succeed at either, but one will cost less daily energy.
Take the evangelist role; type is meaningless so either choice is identical.
ISTJs must never take public-facing roles under any circumstances.
The type determines your ceiling; pick the role matching your type or fail.
scenarios.why: Type-to-role mapping is about sustainable energy, not permission: structured, process-driven operations rewards exactly the ISTJ strengths (thoroughness, dependability, love of order), while constant public performance taxes introverted preferences daily. Both are doable — the question is which role leaves you energized at 6pm. Use the map to predict friction, not to forbid ambition.
scenarios.hint: Which role rewards checklists and deep focus, and which rewards stage presence?

scenarios.title: Composing the founding team
scenarios.situation: You're assembling a three-person founding team and have four candidates' type profiles: an INTJ systems architect, an ENFP evangelist, an ISTJ operator, and an ESTP hustler who thrives in chaos. You can only pick three, and the startup needs product depth, customer energy, and operational discipline in its first year.
scenarios.prompt: What composition principle should guide the pick?
choices: Cover the three working-style bases with complementary strengths — architect (INTJ) for product depth, evangelist (ENFP) for customer energy, operator (ISTJ) for discipline — and manage the known friction points explicitly (e.g., the INTJ's impatience with process vs. the ISTJ's need for it) rather than hoping chemistry handles it.
Pick the three highest-IQ candidates regardless of type; intelligence dominates team outcomes.
Pick three of the same type for maximum alignment and zero friction.
Pick whoever is available first; team composition is overthinking.
scenarios.why: Diverse working styles cover more of the startup's demands than any single profile: the INTJ designs the system, the ENFP sells the vision, the ISTJ keeps the machine running. The value of the typology here is predictive — naming the friction before it happens (independence vs. process, big-picture vs. detail) so the team designs working agreements around it instead of discovering it in a crisis.
scenarios.hint: Which startup job goes unfilled if you drop the ISTJ?

scenarios.title: What it doesn't measure
scenarios.situation: A colleague dismisses the whole instrument: 'It's astrology for HR. It doesn't predict job performance, test-retest reliability is imperfect, and the dichotomies are really continuous traits.' They conclude the assessment is worthless for career planning.
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate middle position?
choices: The criticisms are substantially true — it measures preferences not abilities, the cutoffs are dichotomized continua, and it shouldn't gate hiring — but 'not predictive of performance' doesn't mean 'useless for self-knowledge': as a structured mirror for working style, energy, and blind spots, it earns its place in career reflection alongside skills audits and market data.
The colleague is entirely wrong; the test is scientifically airtight and predicts everything.
The colleague is entirely right; burn the result and never think about working style again.
The test is valid only for extroverts; introverts should use a different instrument.
scenarios.why: Intellectual honesty requires conceding the limits: preferences are not competencies, the four dichotomies slice continuous dimensions, and retest drift happens. But the instrument was never a performance predictor — it's a vocabulary for self-knowledge. Knowing you recharge alone, decide by logic, and need closure before acting is actionable career information even if no peer-reviewed paper blesses the 16 boxes. Use it as one input, never the verdict.
scenarios.hint: If it doesn't predict performance, what CAN it legitimately inform?

scenarios.title: The development plan
scenarios.situation: Your profile is INTJ with strong Thinking and Judging: you decide fast by logic, love systems, and find open-ended emotional conversations draining. Your new role requires leading a team through an ambiguous reorg — exactly the zone your non-preferred side (Feeling, Perceiving) governs: sitting with uncertainty, attuning to people's anxieties, holding plans loosely.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build the development plan?
choices: Name the specific non-preferred muscles the role demands, design low-stakes reps (weekly 1:1s focused on listening not solving, written decision logs that stay open to revision), set observable markers (team reports feeling heard), and review monthly — developing the weaker side while leading from your strengths, not pretending the preferences flipped.
Retake the test until you get ENFJ, then lead naturally.
Avoid the Feeling/Perceiving demands entirely; delegate all people work forever.
Announce to the team that you're an INTJ so they lower their expectations.
scenarios.why: Type development means strengthening the non-preferred functions deliberately, not rewiring your personality: the INTJ's systems thinking becomes the scaffold (structured 1:1s, explicit feedback loops) inside which the weaker muscles get reps. The plan is behavioral and measurable — listening reps, revision-tolerant plans, feedback markers — because 'be more empathetic' is a wish, not a plan.
scenarios.hint: What is one observable marker that your listening reps are working?

lessons.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment — Core concepts
concepts: The instrument: a questionnaire sorting preferences across four dichotomies — Extraversion/Introversion (energy source), Sensing/Intuition (information intake), Thinking/Feeling (decision basis), Judging/Perceiving (orientation to the outer world) — into 16 types. The percentages report preference clarity, not grades.

The 16 types are working styles, not worth ranks: each type names a characteristic pattern of energy, attention, and decision-making. No type is better; each has characteristic strengths and characteristic blind spots.

What it measures: preferences — stable-ish tendencies in how you prefer to work. What it doesn't: ability, intelligence, skills, motivation, mental health, or future job performance. Preference is not competence.

Career-fit mapping uses type to predict energy cost, not to grant permission: match working style to role-family demands (structure vs. ambiguity, people vs. systems, closure vs. exploration) to find roles that energize rather than drain.

Team composition: complementary working styles cover more ground than uniform ones. The typology's team value is predictive — naming friction points (independence vs. process, big-picture vs. detail) so the team designs around them.

The development plan: identify the non-preferred functions your goals demand, build them with deliberate low-stakes reps and observable markers, and lead from your strengths while the weaker side catches up.

example.walkthrough: Each dichotomy is a tug-of-war between its two poles; the winner is the preferred side and the margin — expressed as a percentage — is the preference clarity. The 40.0 next to 'I' mirrors the scenario's 'Introverted (38%)': a moderate signal. A 3% margin would warn you to read both neighboring type descriptions, exactly as the lesson advises.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the four letters as a verdict. The percentages are the actual information — a 3% preference is a near-tie, and the label alone misleads.
Common trap: using preferences as a hiring filter. The instrument measures how people prefer to work, not whether they can do the work — gating on type is misuse.
Common trap: letting type forbid ambition. Mapping predicts energy cost and friction; it never determines what you're allowed to attempt or achieve.
Common trap: confusing the map with the territory. The 16 boxes are a vocabulary for reflection, not a scientific verdict on your potential — pair them with skills audits and real-world feedback.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Build the preference-clarity scorer
labs.objective: Implement the lesson's typology scorer, feed it a realistic 40-answer response set, and produce a full four-dichotomy profile with clarity percentages and near-tie warnings.
steps: Create typer.py with the score_typology function from the lesson.
Build a 40-answer sample: 10 answers per dichotomy with a realistic mix (e.g., EI 7/3, SN 4/6, TF 8/2, JP 5/5).
Print the four dichotomy winners with clarity percentages.
Add near-tie detection: flag any dichotomy with clarity below 15% and print which neighboring type's description to read as well.
Save the printed profile to profile.txt and note in one paragraph what the near-ties change about interpreting the result.

checks.hint: Print all four dichotomy results with their labels.
Print a near-tie warning for low-clarity dichotomies.

labs.title: Working-style team matrix
labs.objective: Write a script that takes a small team's type profiles and prints a working-style coverage matrix: which team strengths are covered, which blind spots are shared, and the top two predicted friction points.
steps: Create team.py with a dict mapping each of the 16 types to 2 strengths and 1 blind spot (write these from the working-styles view: e.g., INTJ -> systems thinking, independence / blind spot: impatience with process).
Define a 4-person team with four different types and print each member's contribution.
Compute shared blind spots: any blind spot appearing in 2+ members gets flagged as a team risk.
Print the top two predicted friction pairs (e.g., J vs P on planning, T vs F on feedback) with a one-line working agreement for each.

checks.hint: Print each member's blind spot explicitly.
Print the predicted friction points with working agreements.

sections.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment — Core path

behavioral.prompt: Describe your working style in two minutes — how you recharge, decide, and organize work.
points: Name your preferences plainly (energy source, decision basis, planning style) with the assessment as vocabulary, not scripture
Give one concrete work example proving each preference
Close with what this means for a team: what you contribute and what support helps you thrive
pitfalls: Reciting four letters with no examples
Presenting preferences as fixed destiny
Only strengths, no blind spots

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you adapted your working style to a teammate who worked very differently.
points: Describe the difference concretely (their style vs. yours) without caricature
Show the specific adaptation: what you changed in communication, planning, or feedback
Name the outcome for the work and what you kept from the experience
pitfalls: Implying their style was wrong and yours was right
A vague 'we communicated better' with no specifics
No lasting change described

behavioral.prompt: What is your biggest working-style blind spot, and how do you manage it?
points: Name the blind spot precisely, tied to your profile (e.g., impatience with process, conflict avoidance)
Show the system that compensates: checklists, scheduled reviews, an accountability partner
Give evidence the system works — a time it caught what you would have missed
pitfalls: A humblebrag blind spot ('I work too hard')
Awareness with no compensating system
Blaming the blind spot for a real failure without owning it

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle conflict with someone whose decision style is the opposite of yours?
points: Show you translate first: restate their position in their decision language (values vs. logic)
Describe separating the people from the problem: shared criteria before positions
Name a real example and the decision mechanism you used
pitfalls: Avoiding conflict entirely
Winning the argument as the goal
No real example

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you led through ambiguity — no clear plan, shifting requirements.
points: Set the ambiguity honestly: what was unknown and what was at stake
Show your method for creating clarity: time-boxed exploration, reversible decisions, explicit assumptions
Name what the team needed from you emotionally, not just technically
pitfalls: Pretending you had a plan all along
Ignoring the human side of ambiguity
No method — just endurance

behavioral.prompt: How do you recharge, and how do you protect that in a demanding role?
points: Name your actual recharge pattern (solitude, people, movement, making things)
Show the boundary system: calendar blocks, rituals, non-negotiables
Connect it to performance: how protected recovery makes your work better
pitfalls: 'I don't need recharge' machismo
No concrete boundary system
Treating rest as weakness

behavioral.prompt: Describe a development goal you're actively working on — a weaker side you're building.
points: Name the specific capability and why your goals demand it
Describe the deliberate reps: frequency, stakes, feedback source
Give the observable marker you'll use to know it's working
pitfalls: A vague goal like 'be more empathetic' with no reps
No marker for progress
Working on a strength and calling it development

behavioral.prompt: Why does self-knowledge matter for the role you're pursuing?
points: Tie specific role demands to your working style honestly — where you fit naturally and where you'll stretch
Show the team value: how your self-knowledge makes you easier to work with
Name what you're still learning about yourself — curiosity over completion
pitfalls: Generic 'self-awareness is important' with no role connection
Claiming perfect fit with no stretch areas
Using the assessment as a credential rather than a mirror

cheatsheet.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment — field reference

sections.heading: The four dichotomies
items: E/I: where you get energy — outer world vs. inner world
S/N: how you take in information — concrete facts vs. patterns
T/F: how you decide — impersonal logic vs. human values
J/P: how you orient outward — closure and plans vs. openness and spontaneity

sections.heading: Reading a result
items: Below ~15% clarity: read the neighboring type too
The letters are shorthand; the full profile is the instrument

sections.heading: Scope discipline
items: Measures: preferences. Does not measure: ability, skill, performance
Use for: self-knowledge, energy management, team design, development
Never for: hiring filters, promotions, worth judgments

sections.heading: From type to plan
items: Map type -> role-family energy fit (friction forecast, not permission)
Compose teams for complementary coverage; name friction early
Develop non-preferred functions with reps + observable markers

glossary.def: A personality framework sorting preferences across four dichotomies into 16 types, originating in Carl Jung's psychological types.
The percentage strength of a reported preference on one dichotomy; low clarity means both sides' descriptions may apply.
The characteristic pattern of energy, attention, and decision-making a type describes — how someone prefers to work.
Whether a person primarily gains energy from the outer world of people and action or the inner world of reflection.
Whether decisions primarily rest on impersonal logic and criteria or on human values and impact.
Whether a person prefers closure, plans, and decidedness or openness, spontaneity, and keeping options open in outer life.
The characteristic weakness of a type — the non-preferred functions it tends to neglect under pressure.
The sides of each dichotomy a person uses less naturally; the target of deliberate development.
